requestedActions.title: List repository names visible to the connected person, with pagination

guide.summary: Forgejo documents an OAuth2 provider using the Authorization Code grant with PKCE, and supports confidential and public clients. Apps are registered in user settings, and the authorize, token and userinfo endpoints are relative to the instance base URL. OAuth2 scopes are explicitly not implemented, so the token can execute any action on behalf of the user; no permission scope is cited. The read action maps to GET /api/v1/repos/search, which lists repositories the user can access with page and limit pagination and x-total-count. GET /api/v1/user/repos is rejected because it lists only repositories the user owns. Setup, token exchange and calls are untested.

findings.title: Forgejo documents an OAuth2 provider with a user-registered app
findings.detail: Forgejo acts as an OAuth2 provider for third-party apps with user consent. Instance-wide apps are created on /admin/applications, while a user can register an app at /user/settings/applications for a Git credential helper or other third-party use.
findings.appliesWhen: Connecting individual customer accounts on their own Forgejo instances.

evidence.quote: OAuth2 provider Forgejo supports acting as an OAuth2 provider to allow third party applications to access its resources with the user’s consent.
Forgejo can act as an instance-wide OAuth2 provider. To achieve that, OAuth2 applications must be created on the /admin/applications page.

findings.title: OAuth2 scopes are not implemented; the token acts with the user's full actions
findings.detail: The documentation states OAuth2 scopes are not yet implemented and OAuth2 tokens can execute any action on behalf of the user. The documented token boundary is therefore the user's own account access, not a read-only scope. Read-only behavior depends on the app.
findings.appliesWhen: Any OAuth2 token issued for this read-only use case.

evidence.quote: OAuth2 scopes are not yet implemented.
Note Scopes are not implemented for OAuth2 tokens and they can be used to
execute any actions on behalf of the user, not just Git-related actions.

findings.title: Register an app, configure the redirect URI and store client credentials
findings.detail: The app must be registered in user settings. A confidential client receives a client ID and secret, while a public client uses PKCE and must be registered as public. Loopback redirect URIs allow any port for public clients. Setup is required before the first test.
findings.appliesWhen: Before the first OAuth authorization test.

evidence.quote: OpenID Connect (OIDC) To use the Authorization Code Grant as a third-party application, it is required to register a new application via the “Settings” ( /user/settings/applications ) section. To test
When created, the OAuth2 application is given a Client ID and a Client secret that https://forgejo.example.com will need to let https://codeberg.org know it is an authorized OAuth2 client.
For public clients, a redirect URI of a loopback IP address such as http://127.0.0.1/ allows any port. Avoid using localhost , as recommended by RFC 8252 .

findings.title: Authorize at the instance base URL and exchange the code for a token
findings.detail: The authorization endpoint is /login/oauth/authorize and the token endpoint is /login/oauth/access_token, both on the customer's instance base URL. The redirect_uri must match between requests. The access token is used as a bearer token for API requests against the user's resources. The connected customer must already have access to the repositories they expect to see.
findings.appliesWhen: Each customer instance connection and test call.

Use the access_token to make API requests to access the user’s resources.
Authorization Endpoint /login/oauth/authorize Access Token Endpoint /login/oauth/access_token

steps.title: Register the OAuth2 app in the customer's Forgejo user settings
steps.detail: In the customer's Forgejo instance, the customer signs in and opens /user/settings/applications to register an OAuth2 application. Choose a confidential client (receives a client ID and secret) or a public client (uses PKCE; must be registered as public). Set the redirect URI to the app's callback URL. Store the client ID and secret in your secret manager; the secret is shown only once. Note: user-registered apps' admin-rights warning in the source refers to instance-wide apps, so the customer should register at user settings, not /admin/applications.
steps.doneWhen: The app appears in the customer's /user/settings/applications list with a client ID and the redirect URI saved.

evidence.quote: OpenID Connect (OIDC) To use the Authorization Code Grant as a third-party application, it is required to register a new application via the “Settings” ( /user/settings/applications ) section. To test
Client types Forgejo supports both confidential and public client types, as defined by RFC 6749 .
For public clients, a redirect URI of a loopback IP address such as http://127.0.0.1/ allows any port. Avoid using localhost , as recommended by RFC 8252 .

fields: INSTANCE_BASE_URL: the customer's full HTTPS Forgejo base URL (user input)
CLIENT_ID and CLIENT_SECRET: from the registered app (user input)
REDIRECT_URI: your app callback URL (user input)

steps.title: Run the authorization-code consent redirect and verify the callback
steps.detail: Open the documented authorization URL in a browser on the customer's instance, with the client ID, redirect URI, response_type=code and a random state. The user approves access and is redirected to REDIRECT_URI with code and state. Verify the returned state matches the value you generated before continuing. This step is a manual user action; do not treat it as completed until the callback is received.
steps.doneWhen: The callback URL contains a code and the same state that was sent.

evidence.quote: Redirect the user to the authorization endpoint in order to get their consent for accessing the resources:
The user will now be asked to authorize your application. If they authorize it, the user will be redirected to the REDIRECT_URL , for example:

fields: INSTANCE_BASE_URL: your full HTTPS instance URL, without a trailing slash
RANDOM_STATE: a random string generated by your app and kept for comparison

steps.title: Exchange the authorization code for an access token
steps.detail: POST to the token endpoint with the returned code, client credentials, grant_type=authorization_code and the same redirect_uri used in the authorize request. Use a confidential client here; a public PKCE client instead sends code_verifier and omits client_secret. The response contains access_token and refresh_token. Store tokens securely. This step is unexecuted until the consent callback has occurred.
steps.doneWhen: The response includes access_token, token_type bearer and expires_in.

steps.title: List visible repositories: first page via GET /api/v1/repos/search
steps.detail: Call the repository search endpoint with limit and page=1 using the bearer token. Repository names are in the data array; read each entry's name field, e.g. $.data[].name. The x-total-count response header gives the total. The endpoint lists repositories the user can access; private defaults to true, so it is set explicitly. GET /api/v1/user/repos is not used because it lists only owned repositories. Read-only: this is a GET request; do not call POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE routes.
steps.doneWhen: The response is 200, ok is true, and data contains repository objects whose name fields are listed. Boundary check: inspect the actual grant against the documented access above; confirm the outgoing request log contains only the requested operations and no prohibited actions.

steps.title: Continue pagination for repository names until the last page
steps.detail: Repeat the search with page=2, 3, and so on, keeping the same limit and filters. Stop when the Link header no longer contains rel="next" or when the collected count reaches x-total-count. A one-page or two-page result is not a full listing unless those conditions are met. Read the same response property $.data[].name on each page.
steps.doneWhen: No rel="next" remains in the Link header, and the collected names equal x-total-count.

steps.title: Confirm the token cannot create, edit or delete repositories (boundary check)
steps.detail: Do not run any write request. Verify the boundary by reviewing the OAuth2 app's authorization in the customer's Forgejo settings and inspecting the outgoing request log for this app, confirming only GET requests to /api/v1/repos/search. Note: OAuth2 scopes are not implemented, so the token can execute any action on behalf of the user; read-only behavior is enforced by your app's code, not by the token.
steps.doneWhen: The app's request log shows only GET calls, and the app code has no write route.

preparation.title: Registration worksheet
preparation.text:
Register the OAuth2 app in the customer's Forgejo user settings
In the customer's Forgejo instance, the customer signs in and opens /user/settings/applications to register an OAuth2 application. Choose a confidential client (receives a client ID and secret) or a public client (uses PKCE; must be registered as public). Set the redirect URI to the app's callback URL. Store the client ID and secret in your secret manager; the secret is shown only once. Note: user-registered apps' admin-rights warning in the source refers to instance-wide apps, so the customer should register at user settings, not /admin/applications.
Fields: INSTANCE_BASE_URL: the customer's full HTTPS Forgejo base URL (user input), CLIENT_ID and CLIENT_SECRET: from the registered app (user input), REDIRECT_URI: your app callback URL (user input)

Exchange the authorization code for an access token
